$$\max_{\vec\alpha\,\geq\,0}\;\vec\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\,\vec\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\vec\alpha$$

Support vector machines: from a constrained problem to the points that decide it

Lagrange multipliers turn a constraint into a price. Applied to the widest possible margin between two classes, those prices vanish for almost every training point, and the handful that remain define the classifier.

Part A
Lagrangian optimisation
1

Constrained optimisation

Find the lowest point of a function — but only among the points that obey a rule.

The problem this whole topic is built around has two parts: a function to minimise and a condition the answer must satisfy.

$$\min_{w}\; f(w)\qquad \text{s.t.}\qquad g(w)\le 0$$
  • \(f(w)\) is the objective function — what we want to make small.
  • \(g(w)\) is the constraint function. The set of points it allows, \(\mathcal F=\{w : g(w)\le 0\}\), is the feasible set.

Without the constraint we would set \(\nabla f(w)=0\) and be done. With it, that stationary point may lie outside \(\mathcal F\), and the true answer may sit on the boundary \(g(w)=0\) where \(\nabla f\neq 0\). We can attack this directly, or find a reformulation that is easier to solve. The Lagrangian is that reformulation: it folds the constraint into the objective so that the outer problem over \(w\) has no constraint left.

The standard form and its conventions

Every problem in these notes is first rewritten into the shape above. Two conventions make that possible:

  • Always minimise. Maximising \(h(w)\) is the same as minimising \(-h(w)\), or — when \(h>0\) — minimising \(1/h(w)\). Block 12 uses the second trick.
  • Always write constraints as "something \(\le 0\)". A constraint \(h(w)\ge c\) becomes \(c-h(w)\le 0\). Block 13 does exactly this with the SVM constraint \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\).

Real problems have many constraints \(g_1(w)\le 0,\dots,g_n(w)\le 0\). The lecture develops the theory with one constraint for readability; everything generalises by giving each constraint its own multiplier, which is what the SVM needs — one constraint per training point.

Why the sign convention matters

The multiplier introduced in the next block is required to be non-negative. That requirement only makes sense if every constraint is written as \(g(w)\le 0\). Writing a constraint the other way round silently flips the sign of its multiplier and breaks every argument in blocks 3 to 7.

2

The Lagrangian function

Add the constraint to the objective, scaled by a non-negative weight.

$$L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha\,g(w),\qquad \alpha\ge 0$$

The new variable \(\alpha\) is the Lagrange multiplier. We still optimise over \(w\), but \(L\) now also depends on \(\alpha\). A useful way to read \(\alpha\) is as a price per unit of violation: whenever \(g(w)>0\) the term \(\alpha\,g(w)\) charges for breaking the rule, and a larger \(\alpha\) charges more.

With \(n\) constraints there is one multiplier per constraint, collected into a vector \(\vec\alpha\):

$$L(w,\vec\alpha)=f(w)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,g_i(w),\qquad \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0$$

If we fix a \(w\), we can ask how large the Lagrangian can be made by choosing \(\alpha\):

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,L(w,\alpha)=\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)$$

The answer to that question, worked out in the next block, is what makes the whole construction work.

3

What maximising over α does

For a fixed \(w\), the inner maximum is either infinite or exactly \(f(w)\) — and which one depends only on whether \(w\) is feasible.

Case 1: \(g(w)>0\) — the constraint is violated

The term \(\alpha\,g(w)\) is a positive number times \(\alpha\). Since we are maximising, we increase \(\alpha\) without limit, which pushes \(L(w,\alpha)\to\infty\).

Case 2: \(g(w)\le 0\) — the constraint is satisfied

Now \(\alpha\,g(w)\le 0\) for every \(\alpha\ge 0\): any positive \(\alpha\) can only lower \(L\) (or leave it unchanged when \(g(w)=0\)). The best choice is \(\alpha=0\), which gives \(L(w,\alpha)=f(w)\).

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}L(w,\alpha)=\begin{cases}\;\infty, & g(w)>0\\[4pt] \;f(w), & g(w)\le 0\end{cases}$$

In effect, \(\max_{\alpha}\) builds an infinitely high wall around the feasible set and leaves \(f\) untouched inside it. The constraint has not disappeared — it has been turned into part of the objective.

Correction

The lecture's region diagram labels the feasible set with \(L(w,\alpha)=g(w)\). It should read \(\max_{\alpha}L(w,\alpha)=f(w)\), as the case analysis above shows.

The slide also says that \(\alpha\,g(w)\) "will always be negative if \(\alpha>0\)". It is non-positive: when the constraint is exactly tight, \(g(w)=0\), the term is zero for every \(\alpha\). That boundary case is not a technicality — it is where the SVM's support vectors live (block 17).

4

The primal: a min–max problem

Minimise the result of block 3 over \(w\), and you get back exactly the problem you started with.

We originally wanted the \(w\) that minimises \(f(w)\) subject to \(g(w)\le 0\). Take the function from block 3 and minimise it over \(w\). The outer minimisation will never choose an infeasible \(w\), because those score \(\infty\); among feasible ones it sees exactly \(f(w)\). So the two problems have the same solution:

$$\underbrace{\min_{w}\, f(w)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ g(w)\le 0}_{\text{original problem}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\min_{w}\,\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)}_{\text{Lagrangian equivalent (primal)}}$$

The min–max form is called the primal. Its optimal value is written \(p^\star\) and its minimiser \(w^{\text{opt}}\) (also written \(w^\star\)). Notice the outer problem over \(w\) is now unconstrained — the only constraint left is the trivial \(\alpha\ge 0\) on the inner variable.

Why not just pick one large fixed penalty, say \(\alpha=1000\), and minimise \(f(w)+1000\,g(w)\)?

Any fixed, finite \(\alpha\) lets a slightly infeasible \(w\) win if \(f\) drops by more than the penalty charged. The inner maximisation removes that loophole: for every infeasible \(w\) it chooses a price high enough to make it lose. It is an exact penalty, not an approximate one.

5

Swapping min and max: the dual

Doing the minimisation over \(w\) first often turns out to be much easier. The question is whether it gives the same answer.

We converted a minimisation into a min–max problem. Before going further, the lecture poses two questions. The first is whether the order of min and max can be exchanged:

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\Bigl(\min_{w}\,L(w,\alpha)\Bigr)$$

Dual form

$$\min_{w}\,\Bigl(\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,L(w,\alpha)\Bigr)$$

Primal form

The inner part of the dual has a name. The dual function is

$$q(\alpha)=\min_{w}\,L(w,\alpha)=\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr),$$

and the dual problem is \(\max_{\alpha\ge 0}q(\alpha)\), with optimal value \(d^\star\) and maximiser \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\). The second question — the slide promises two but only states one — is what the swap buys us and how to get \(w\) back from \(\alpha\). Part C answers both for the SVM.

Weak duality: always true

Without any assumption on \(f\) or \(g\), the dual can never exceed the primal. Take any feasible \(w\) and any \(\alpha\ge 0\):

$$q(\alpha)=\min_{w'}L(w',\alpha)\;\le\;L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\underbrace{\alpha\,g(w)}_{\le\,0}\;\le\; f(w).$$

The left side does not depend on \(w\) and the right side does not depend on \(\alpha\), so we may maximise the left over \(\alpha\) and minimise the right over feasible \(w\):

$$d^\star=\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)\;\le\;\min_{w}\max_{\alpha\ge 0}L(w,\alpha)=p^\star$$

The difference \(p^\star-d^\star\ge 0\) is the duality gap. A second fact that holds unconditionally: \(q(\alpha)\) is always concave, because it is a minimum of functions that are linear in \(\alpha\). The dual is therefore always a well-behaved maximisation, even when the primal is not.

Strong duality: when the gap closes

When \(d^\star=p^\star\) we have strong duality, and solving the dual is as good as solving the primal. The standard sufficient condition is:

  • \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are convex, and
  • Slater's condition holds: some \(w\) satisfies every constraint strictly, \(g_i(w)<0\). When the constraints are affine, as they are for the SVM, plain feasibility is enough.
Correction

The slide states: "If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex, then we can interchange min and max. Else, we cannot." Two refinements. Convexity alone is not quite sufficient — a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition is also needed, although it is almost always satisfied in machine-learning problems. And without convexity the swap is not forbidden; it is merely no longer guaranteed. What always survives is the inequality \(d^\star\le p^\star\).

PrimalDual
Form\(\min_w\max_{\alpha\ge0}L\)\(\max_{\alpha\ge0}\min_w L\)
Optimised variable\(w\) (outer)\(\alpha\) (outer)
Optimal value\(p^\star\)\(d^\star\le p^\star\) always
Shapeconvex if \(f,g\) areconcave in \(\alpha\), always
Equal when\(f,g\) convex and Slater's condition holds

This is why the lecture checked all this before touching the SVM: the SVM primal will turn out to be convex with affine constraints, so we are free to solve its dual instead — and the dual is easier.

6

Worked example: one variable, one constraint

A problem small enough to solve both ways by hand.

Minimise \(w^2\) subject to \(w\ge 1\). In standard form the constraint is \(g(w)=1-w\le 0\), so

$$L(w,\alpha)=w^2+\alpha\,(1-w),\qquad \alpha\ge 0.$$

Primal, directly

The unconstrained minimum of \(w^2\) is at \(w=0\), which is infeasible. The objective increases for \(w>0\), so the best feasible point is on the boundary: \(w^\star=1\), \(p^\star=1\).

Dual

For fixed \(\alpha\), minimise over \(w\): \(\partial L/\partial w=2w-\alpha=0\) gives \(w_\alpha=\alpha/2\). Substituting back,

$$q(\alpha)=\frac{\alpha^2}{4}+\alpha\Bigl(1-\frac{\alpha}{2}\Bigr)=\alpha-\frac{\alpha^2}{4}.$$

Maximising, \(q'(\alpha)=1-\alpha/2=0\) gives \(\alpha^\star=2\) and \(d^\star=q(2)=1\). So \(d^\star=p^\star\): strong duality, as expected for a convex problem. And the primal solution is recovered from the dual one through the inner minimiser: \(w_{\alpha^\star}=\alpha^\star/2=1\).

Repeat the example with the constraint \(w\ge -1\). What is \(\alpha^\star\)?

Now \(g(w)=-1-w\). The inner minimiser is still \(w_\alpha=\alpha/2\), and \(q(\alpha)=-\alpha-\alpha^2/4\), which is largest at \(\alpha^\star=0\) with \(d^\star=0\). The unconstrained minimum \(w=0\) is already feasible, so the constraint is irrelevant and its price is zero. This is complementary slackness, the subject of the next block.

7

Complementary slackness and the KKT conditions

At the optimum, every constraint is either tight or free — never both slack and priced.

Assume strong duality, and let \(w^{\text{opt}}\) solve the primal and \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) solve the dual. Substitute each into its own problem:

$$\max_{\alpha\ge0}\bigl(f(w^{\text{opt}})+\alpha\,g(w^{\text{opt}})\bigr)\;=\;\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\bigr)$$

On the left, \(w^{\text{opt}}\) is feasible, so by block 3 the maximum is simply \(f(w^{\text{opt}})\):

$$f(w^{\text{opt}})=\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\bigr)$$

The right side is the minimum of \(L(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}})\) over all \(w\). The particular point \(w^{\text{opt}}\) is one of the candidates, but not necessarily the minimiser, so its value is at least as large as the minimum:

$$f(w^{\text{opt}})\;\le\;f(w^{\text{opt}})+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\ge 0\quad (1)$$

But the constraints themselves say \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\ge 0\) and \(g(w^{\text{opt}})\le 0\), so their product satisfies

$$\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\le 0\quad (2)$$

Inequalities (1) and (2) can hold together only if the product is zero:

$$\alpha^{\text{opt}}\cdot g\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)=0\qquad\text{(complementary slackness)}$$

Read it as a pair of alternatives. Either the multiplier is zero — the constraint is inactive and could be deleted without changing the answer — or \(g(w^{\text{opt}})=0\), the constraint is active and the solution sits exactly on its boundary. Both factors may be zero at once. In the example of block 6, \(\alpha^\star=2>0\) and \(g(1)=0\); in its variant, \(\alpha^\star=0\) and \(g(0)=-1<0\).

With several constraints the same argument gives \(\sum_i\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}g_i(w^{\text{opt}})\ge0\) while every term is \(\le 0\), so each term vanishes separately: \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}g_i(w^{\text{opt}})=0\) for every \(i\).

Correction

This derivation appears in the SVM lecture under "Equating primal and dual" and has been moved here, since it holds for any problem with strong duality. The slide describes the curve as "the convex graph for the dual: \(y=w^2\), i.e. \(y=f(w^2)\)" and says "for the dual, we need to minimise \(w\)". More precisely: the curve illustrates the inner objective \(w\mapsto L(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}})\), and the dual minimises that function over \(w\).

The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions

Complementary slackness is one of four conditions that together characterise the optimum. For convex problems satisfying Slater's condition they are both necessary and sufficient:

ConditionStatementWhere it comes from
Stationarity\(\nabla f(w^\star)+\sum_i\alpha_i^\star\nabla g_i(w^\star)=0\)\(w^\star\) minimises \(L(w,\alpha^\star)\)
Primal feasibility\(g_i(w^\star)\le 0\) for all \(i\)the original constraints
Dual feasibility\(\alpha_i^\star\ge 0\) for all \(i\)the multipliers' sign
Complementary slackness\(\alpha_i^\star\,g_i(w^\star)=0\) for all \(i\)the argument above

For the SVM, stationarity will give the formula for \(w\) (block 14) and complementary slackness will identify the support vectors (block 17).

Part B
The maximum-margin problem
8

Many separators, one margin

A linearly separable dataset has infinitely many separating lines. Which one should we prefer?

Here is one dataset with three separating lines, each drawn with its margin band \(w^{\top}x=\pm\gamma\):

All three classify the training data perfectly. Intuitively, separator 3 is the best: its band is widest, so a new point that lands a little away from its class's training points is still likely to fall on the correct side. The perceptron gives a formal version of that intuition.

The perceptron's mistake bound

If the data is separable with margin \(\gamma\) and every point satisfies \(\lVert x_i\rVert\le R\), the number of mistakes \(l\) the perceptron makes before converging is bounded by

$$l\;\le\;\left(\frac{R}{\gamma}\right)^{2}$$

A larger margin means fewer mistakes. But the perceptron only guarantees that it will find some \(w\) that separates the data with some positive margin — which one depends on the initialisation and on the order the examples arrive in. It does not guarantee the \(w\) with the maximum margin. So we need a method that searches for that one explicitly.

Functional margin and geometric margin

Two different quantities are both called "margin", and the slides move between them. The functional margin of a point is \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\); the geometric margin is \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i/\lVert w\rVert\), the actual distance from the point to the line. In the mistake bound, \(\gamma\) is geometric (it assumes \(\lVert w\rVert=1\)). In the three figures, \(\gamma\) is functional: the dashed lines are \(w^{\top}x=\pm\gamma\), and the band's real half-width is \(\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\).

Separator\(w\)\(\gamma\) (functional)\(\lVert w\rVert\)half-width \(\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\)band width
1\([1,\,1]\)11.4140.7071.414
2\([1,\,0.5]\)1.51.1181.3422.683
3\([0.5,\,1]\)21.1181.7893.578

Here the ranking by \(\gamma\) happens to agree with the ranking by true width. In general it need not: \(\gamma\) alone says nothing until \(\lVert w\rVert\) is pinned down. That observation is the whole of the next block.

9

The naive formulation is ill-posed

Maximise the margin, subject to every point clearing it. Written literally, this has no solution.

The direct translation of "find the boundary that maximises \(\gamma\)" is

$$\max_{w,\,\gamma}\;\gamma\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge\gamma\quad\forall i$$

Suppose \((w,\gamma)\) satisfies every constraint. Multiply through by any \(c>0\):

$$y_i\,(cw)^{\top}x_i=c\,y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\;\ge\;c\gamma\qquad\forall i$$

so \((cw,\,c\gamma)\) satisfies them too. For \(c>1\) the objective has grown, \(c\gamma>\gamma\), yet the decision boundary \(\{x : (cw)^{\top}x=0\}\) is the same set of points as \(\{x : w^{\top}x=0\}\). Nothing about the geometry has changed.

Because the constraints allow a larger \(\gamma\) whenever \(w\) is scaled up, the optimisation drives both \(\gamma\) and \(\lVert w\rVert\) to infinity without ever changing the separator. The problem is unbounded — it has no optimal solution — and is called ill-posed. To make it meaningful we must remove the freedom to scale \(w\) arbitrarily. There are two ways to do it, in the next two blocks.

Where did the bias go?

The figure above includes a bias \(b\), but the lecture's algebra uses \(w^{\top}x\) alone, which describes a boundary through the origin. The usual justification is to append a constant feature, \(x\mapsto[x;\,1]\), so that the last weight plays the role of \(b\). That is fine for classification, but it means the norm \(\lVert w\rVert^2\) minimised later also includes \(b^2\), which is a slightly different problem from the standard SVM. The standard version keeps \(b\) separate; blocks 15 and 19 note what changes when it does.

10

Fix 1: fix the norm of w

Only allow weight vectors of unit length. Correct, but awkward to optimise.

Add the constraint \(\lVert w\rVert_2^2=1\). If \((w,\gamma)\) is feasible, the scaled pair \((cw,c\gamma)\) now has \(\lVert cw\rVert_2^2=c^2\lVert w\rVert_2^2=c^2\), which violates the constraint for every \(c\neq1\). Scaling is ruled out.

$$\max_{w,\,\gamma}\;\gamma\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge\gamma\ \ \forall i\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lVert w\rVert_2^2=1$$

With a unit-length \(w\), \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\) is the true distance of \(x_i\) from the boundary, so \(\gamma\) is now the geometric margin. The formulation is correct. It is just inconvenient:

  • We optimise over two kinds of variable, \(w\) and \(\gamma\), coupled through every constraint.
  • The set \(\{w : \lVert w\rVert=1\}\) is a sphere, which is not a convex set: the midpoint of two unit vectors is shorter than 1. An equality constraint keeps a problem convex only if it is affine. Without convexity, the duality results of block 5 are no longer guaranteed, and it is the dual we want to solve later.
An aside

Relaxing the equality to \(\lVert w\rVert\le 1\) makes the problem convex again, because the unit ball is a convex set, and the optimum always lands on its boundary anyway. The lecture takes a different route, which leads to a cleaner objective.

11

Fix 2: fix the functional margin to 1

Instead of fixing the length of \(w\), fix the value of \(\gamma\) — and let the length of \(w\) carry the information.

A three-dimensional example

Take \(w=[2,\,4,\,3]\) and \(\gamma=10\), so \(w^{\top}x=2x_1+4x_2+3x_3\). The three planes \(w^{\top}x=10\), \(w^{\top}x=0\) and \(w^{\top}x=-10\) are parallel, each perpendicular to \(w\).

The distance between two parallel planes \(w^{\top}x=0\) and \(w^{\top}x=\gamma\) follows from moving along the unit normal. Start at any \(x_0\) with \(w^{\top}x_0=0\) and step a distance \(t\) in the direction \(w/\lVert w\rVert\):

$$w^{\top}\Bigl(x_0+t\,\frac{w}{\lVert w\rVert}\Bigr)=0+t\,\frac{w^{\top}w}{\lVert w\rVert}=t\,\lVert w\rVert=\gamma\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=\frac{\gamma}{\lVert w\rVert}$$

Here \(\operatorname{len}(\overline{AB})=\operatorname{len}(\overline{CD})=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2^2+4^2+3^2}}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{29}}\approx1.857\).

Rescaling so that \(\gamma=1\)

Now divide \(w\) by \(10\). With \(w_{\text{new}}=w/10\), the same three planes are described by

$$\frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{10}{10}=1,\qquad \frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{0}{10}=0,\qquad \frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{-10}{10}=-1.$$

This is always possible. Whichever \(w\) separates the dataset, it can be rescaled so that the closest points satisfy \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i=1\) exactly — a canonical scaling. So we may require

$$y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\qquad\forall i$$

Different separators need different rescalings

Applying the same idea to separators 2 and 3 from block 8:

Separatordivide \(w\) by\(w_{\text{new}}\)\(\lVert w_{\text{new}}\rVert\)half-width \(1/\lVert w_{\text{new}}\rVert\)
11\([1,\,1]\)1.4140.707
21.5\([0.667,\,0.333]\)0.7451.342
32\([0.25,\,0.5]\)0.5591.789
The key observation

A larger margin means dividing \(w\) by a larger number, which makes \(w_{\text{new}}\) smaller. Once the functional margin is fixed at 1, the width of the band is controlled entirely by \(\lVert w\rVert\): the smaller the weight vector, the wider the margin.

12

Maximum width and the convex primal

Among all canonically scaled separators, choose the one with the widest band.

Every separating \(w\) can be scaled to satisfy \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\). We prefer the one that leaves the most room between the two margin lines:

$$\max_{w}\;\operatorname{width}(w)\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\quad\forall i$$

From block 11, each margin line is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\) from the boundary, so the width between \(w^{\top}x=1\) and \(w^{\top}x=-1\) is \(2/\lVert w\rVert\).

So we maximise \(2/\lVert w\rVert\). Equivalently we may maximise \(2/\lVert w\rVert^2\): squaring is strictly increasing for positive numbers, so both objectives are largest at the same \(w\). And maximising a positive quantity is the same as minimising its reciprocal:

$$\max_{w}\frac{2}{\lVert w\rVert^2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\min_{w}\frac{\lVert w\rVert^2}{2}$$
$$\min_{w}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\quad\forall i$$

This is the hard-margin SVM primal. The objective is a convex quadratic; each constraint is affine in \(w\). It is a quadratic program with a unique optimal \(w\), and it has a feasible point exactly when the data is linearly separable. The factor \(\tfrac12\) changes nothing about the answer; it is there so that the gradient of the objective is simply \(w\).

Correction

The slide justifies replacing \(2/\lVert w\rVert\) by \(2/\lVert w\rVert^2\) with "because we are just scaling the constraint". The actual reason is monotonicity: \(t\mapsto t^2\) preserves order for \(t>0\), so the maximiser does not change even though the optimal value does. No constraint is being scaled at this step.

With a separate bias the primal reads \(\min_{w,b}\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to \(y_i\,(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge1\). Only \(w\) is penalised, so shifting the boundary is free and only tilting it costs.

Why minimise \(\lVert w\rVert^2\) instead of \(\lVert w\rVert\), when both give the same \(w\)?

\(\lVert w\rVert\) has a kink at \(w=0\) and a gradient \(w/\lVert w\rVert\) that is awkward to work with. \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) is smooth everywhere with gradient \(w\), which is what makes the inner minimisation in block 14 a one-line calculation and turns the whole problem into a standard quadratic program.

Part C
The dual and the support vectors
13

The SVM in Lagrangian form

Rewrite the primal in the standard shape of block 1, and Part A applies directly.

The SVM primal is solvable as it stands — it is a quadratic program. But looking at it through the Lagrangian lens gives a problem that is often easier and, more importantly, far more revealing. First, match it to the standard form \(\min_w f(w)\) s.t. \(g_i(w)\le0\):

StepForm
Primal from block 12\(\min_w \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\ \ \forall i\)
Constraints moved to "\(\le 0\)"\(\min_w \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ 1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\le 0\ \ \forall i\)
Matched to the standard form\(f(w)=\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2,\qquad g_i(w)=1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\)

There is one constraint per training point, so there are \(n\) multipliers \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\). The primal in min–max form is

$$\min_{w}\;\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\Bigl(\,{\color{#4A1E5C}\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2}\;+\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\color{#1F8A85}\alpha_i}\,{\color{#B23A6B}\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)}\Bigr)$$
objective \(f(w)\)Small \(\lVert w\rVert\) means a wide margin.
multiplier \(\alpha_i\)One price per training point, \(\alpha_i\ge0\).
constraint \(g_i(w)\)Positive exactly when point \(i\) is inside the margin or misclassified.

Is swapping to the dual allowed? \(f\) is convex, every \(g_i\) is affine, and for separable data a feasible \(w\) exists. By block 5, strong duality holds, so the dual has the same optimal value:

$$\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\min_{w}\;\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\Bigr)$$
Correction

The slide's standard optimisation form writes the constraint as \(g(w_i)\le 0\). The index belongs to the constraint, not to \(w\): there is a single weight vector and \(n\) constraint functions, \(g_i(w)\le 0\).

14

Solving the inner minimisation

For fixed multipliers, the best \(w\) is a weighted sum of the training points.

Fix \(\vec\alpha\) — say \(n=3\) and \(\alpha_1=3,\ \alpha_2=0,\ \alpha_3=8\). What remains is

$$\min_{w}\;\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\Bigr)$$

This is an unconstrained minimisation over \(w\) of a convex, differentiable function — the same situation as finding the \(w\) that minimises squared loss in linear regression. So we differentiate with respect to \(w\) and set the result to zero. Expanding the sum first:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w}\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\Bigr)=w-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,x_i=0$$
$$\vec w_{\alpha}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,\vec x_i$$

This is the stationarity condition of block 7. With \(\alpha=(3,0,8)\) it gives \(w_\alpha=3y_1x_1+8y_3x_3\): the point \(x_2\) plays no part at all. That observation becomes the central result of block 17.

The result depends on \(\alpha\), and the outer problem is still to find the \(\alpha\) that maximises the objective. So the next step is to substitute \(w_\alpha\) back into the objective, leaving a function of \(\alpha\) alone.

Matrix form

Stack the data points as the rows of \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\), put the labels on the diagonal of \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(y_1,\dots,y_n)\), and collect the multipliers in \(\vec\alpha\in\mathbb R^{n}\). Then \(X^{\top}\) has the data points as its columns, and

$$\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} w_{1}\\ w_{2}\\ \vdots\\ w_{d}\end{bmatrix}}_{d\times 1} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1} & x_{2,1} & \cdots & x_{n,1}\\ x_{1,2} & x_{2,2} & \cdots & x_{n,2}\\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\ x_{1,d} & x_{2,d} & \cdots & x_{n,d}\end{bmatrix}}_{d\times n\;=\;X^{\top}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} y_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\ 0 & y_2 & \cdots & 0\\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots\\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & y_n\end{bmatrix}}_{n\times n\;=\;Y} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2\\ \vdots\\ \alpha_n\end{bmatrix}}_{n\times 1}$$

\(x_{i,j}\) is feature \(j\) of data point \(i\). Column \(i\) of \(X^{\top}\) is \(\vec x_i\); multiplying by \(Y\) scales it to \(y_i\vec x_i\), and multiplying by \(\vec\alpha\) sums the columns with weights \(\alpha_i\).

$$\vec w_{\alpha}=X^{\top}Y\,\vec\alpha$$
Correction

In the slide's matrix picture the columns of \(X^{\top}\) are labelled \(x_{1,\cdot},x_{2,\cdot},\dots,x_{d,\cdot}\) and the rows run down to index \(n\). The two dimensions are swapped: \(X^{\top}\) is \(d\times n\), so it has \(n\) columns (one per data point) and \(d\) rows (one per feature), as in the version above.

15

Back-substitution: the dual objective

Replace \(w\) by \(X^{\top}Y\vec\alpha\) everywhere, and the problem becomes a quadratic in \(\alpha\) alone.

In matrix notation, the vector with entries \(1-y_i\,x_i^{\top}w\) is \(\mathbf 1-YXw\), so the Lagrangian is

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)=\tfrac12\,w_\alpha^{\top}w_\alpha+\alpha^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf 1-YXw_\alpha\bigr)$$

Substituting \(w_\alpha=X^{\top}Y\alpha\):

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)={\color{#1F8A85}\tfrac12\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)}+{\color{#B8582A}\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1}-{\color{#B23A6B}\alpha^{\top}YX\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)}$$

Simplify each coloured term. Since \(Y\) is diagonal, \(Y^{\top}=Y\):

TermSimplification
①\(\tfrac12\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)=\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}Y^{\top}X\,X^{\top}Y\alpha=\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\)
②\(\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1=\sum_i\alpha_i\) — already as simple as it gets
③\(\alpha^{\top}YX\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)=\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\) — the same quadratic form as ①, without the \(\tfrac12\)

So ① − ③ is \(\bigl(\tfrac12-1\bigr)\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\), and

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)=\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha$$

Maximising this over \(\alpha\ge0\) is the SVM dual. Written out with sums, which is how it usually appears in exam questions:

$$\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,x_i^{\top}x_j$$

The matrix \(K=XX^{\top}\), with entries \(K_{ij}=x_i^{\top}x_j\), is the Gram matrix of the data. The matrix \(Q=YXX^{\top}Y=(YX)(YX)^{\top}\) is positive semi-definite, so \(-\tfrac12\alpha^{\top}Q\alpha\) is concave: the dual is a concave quadratic maximisation over the simple region \(\alpha\ge0\).

With a separate bias \(b\)

If the constraints are \(y_i(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge 1\), the Lagrangian gains a term \(-b\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\). Setting its derivative with respect to \(b\) to zero gives one extra condition, and the dual becomes the same objective with the constraints

$$\alpha_i\ge 0\ \ \forall i\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i=0.$$

The second constraint says the total price on each class must balance. This is the form found in most textbooks and in library implementations.

16

Why the dual helps

The same problem, stated in terms of data points instead of features.

$$\min_{w}\ \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1$$

Standard primal: \(d\) variables

$$\max_{\vec\alpha\ge 0}\ \alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha$$

Standard dual: \(n\) variables

The primal searches over \(w\in\mathbb R^{d}\), one variable per feature. The dual searches over \(\alpha\in\mathbb R^{n}\), one variable per training point. When \(d\gg n\) — text with a vocabulary of a million words and a few thousand documents, for instance — the dual solves the same problem in far fewer dimensions.

What the dual gains
  • Dimension \(n\) instead of \(d\).
  • Constraints are just \(\alpha_i\ge0\), instead of \(n\) coupled inequalities.
  • The data enters only through inner products \(x_i^{\top}x_j\), which is what makes kernels possible (block 21).
  • Most \(\alpha_i\) come out exactly zero (block 17), so the solution is sparse.
What it costs
  • The Gram matrix is \(n\times n\): memory grows as \(n^2\).
  • When \(n\gg d\), the primal is the smaller problem.
  • \(w\) is not produced directly; it has to be rebuilt from \(\alpha\) through \(w=X^{\top}Y\alpha\).
17

Complementary slackness: the support vectors

Only the points on the margin get a non-zero price. They alone determine \(w\).

From block 14, the optimal weight vector is a linear combination of the data points, with the importance of point \(i\) given by \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\ge 0\):

$$\vec w_{\alpha^{\text{opt}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\,y_i\,\vec x_i$$

Some \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\) may be zero and others positive. Which ones? Apply complementary slackness (block 7) to the SVM constraint \(g_i(w)=1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\):

$$\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\times\Bigl(1-y_i\,\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)^{\top}x_i\Bigr)=0\qquad\forall i$$

Each product is zero, which leaves two readings:

If \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}>0\)
$$1-y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i=0$$ $$\Rightarrow\ y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i=1$$

The point lies exactly on its margin line.

If \(y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i>1\)
$$1-y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i<0$$ $$\Rightarrow\ \alpha_i^{\text{opt}}=0$$

The point is strictly beyond its margin line and contributes nothing.

Only points on the margin can have \(\alpha_i>0\), so only they contribute to \(w^{\text{opt}}\). These points are called support vectors — they "support" the margin the way the posts support a fence — and the algorithm is the support vector machine. The rest of the training set could be thrown away after training.

Corrections

Sign slip. On the second support-vector slide the right-hand branch reads \(\bigl(1-(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_iy_i\bigr)>0\Rightarrow\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}=0\). It should be \(<0\), as on the slide before it. A positive value would mean the constraint is violated, which cannot happen at a feasible optimum.

The implication runs one way. The slide concludes that "only the points on the gamma margin will have alpha > 0". The logic gives \(\alpha_i>0\Rightarrow\) on the margin, but not the converse: a point can lie exactly on the margin and still have \(\alpha_i=0\), because both factors of the product may be zero. Support vectors are the points with \(\alpha_i>0\); they all lie on the margin, but not every margin point must be one. When several margin points are collinear, as in the figure, the optimal \(\alpha\) is often not unique even though \(w\) is (block 18 shows this).

The illustration is schematic. For the points as drawn, the diagonal band is not actually the widest one. Every support vector must satisfy \(w=\sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i\), and no non-negative combination of the circled points gives a \(w\) in the direction \((1,1)\). Solving the QP on these points gives the vertical boundary \(x_1=0\), with support vectors \((-1,0)\) and \((1,0)\) and width \(2\), wider than the drawn band's \(\sqrt2\). The figure still conveys the right idea: only points on the margin carry weight.

18

Worked example: three points by hand

Solve a small dual completely and check every claim of Part C against it.

Point\(x_i\)\(y_i\)\(u_i=y_ix_i\)
1\((1,\,1)\)\(+1\)\((1,\,1)\)
2\((-1,\,-1)\)\(-1\)\((1,\,1)\)
3\((2,\,3)\)\(+1\)\((2,\,3)\)

Step 1 — build \(Q=YXX^{\top}Y\)

Its entries are \(Q_{ij}=y_iy_j\,x_i^{\top}x_j=u_i^{\top}u_j\):

$$Q=\begin{bmatrix}2&2&5\\2&2&5\\5&5&13\end{bmatrix}$$

Step 2 — maximise the dual

Point 3 is far from the boundary, so guess \(\alpha_3=0\) and check it afterwards. With \(s=\alpha_1+\alpha_2\), the dual objective becomes

$$s-\tfrac12\cdot 2s^2=s-s^2,$$

which is maximised at \(s=\tfrac12\).

Step 3 — recover \(w\) and check

$$w=\alpha_1u_1+\alpha_2u_2=s\,(1,1)=\bigl(\tfrac12,\,\tfrac12\bigr)$$

Check the constraints: \(y_1w^{\top}x_1=1\), \(y_2w^{\top}x_2=1\), and \(y_3w^{\top}x_3=2.5>1\). Points 1 and 2 are on the margin; point 3 is beyond it, so \(\alpha_3=0\) is consistent with complementary slackness. The partial derivative of the dual with respect to \(\alpha_3\) at this point is \(1-(Q\alpha)_3=1-5\cdot\tfrac12<0\), so raising \(\alpha_3\) would only lower the objective: the guess was right.

The margin width is \(2/\lVert w\rVert=2/(1/\sqrt2)=2\sqrt2\), which equals the distance between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), as it must when they are the only support vectors.

Unique \(w\), non-unique \(\alpha\)

In the lecture's bias-free form, the dual only fixes \(\alpha_1+\alpha_2=\tfrac12\). Any split — \((\tfrac12,0)\), \((\tfrac14,\tfrac14)\), \((0,\tfrac12)\) — gives the same \(w\), because \(u_1=u_2\). In the first split, \(x_2\) sits on the margin with \(\alpha_2=0\): a margin point that is not a support vector, exactly the case described in block 17. With a separate bias the extra constraint \(\alpha_1y_1+\alpha_2y_2=0\) forces \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\tfrac14\), and \(b=y_1-w^{\top}x_1=0\).

If \(x_3\) were deleted from the training set, would the classifier change? What if \(x_1\) were deleted?

Deleting \(x_3\) changes nothing: it has \(\alpha_3=0\) and is not in the sum for \(w\). Deleting \(x_1\) changes the problem: the only positive point left is \(x_3=(2,3)\), whose distance from \(x_2\) is larger, so the margin widens and \(w\) changes. Support vectors are exactly the points the solution cannot do without.

19

Training and prediction

Everything above reduces to two phases.

Training phase

  1. Solve the dual QP of block 15 for \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\).
  2. Compute \(w^{\text{opt}}=\sum_i\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}y_ix_i\). Only the support vectors (\(\alpha_i>0\)) enter the sum.
  3. If the model has a bias, take any support vector \(x_s\): from \(y_s(w^{\top}x_s+b)=1\) and \(y_s^2=1\), \(b=y_s-w^{\top}x_s\). In practice this is averaged over all support vectors for numerical stability.

Testing phase

For a new point \(x_{\text{test}}\), compute

$$f(x_{\text{test}})=\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)^{\top}x_{\text{test}}=\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{SV}}\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\,y_i\;x_i^{\top}x_{\text{test}}$$
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})>0\), predict \(y=+1\).
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})<0\), predict \(y=-1\).
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})=0\) the point lies on the boundary itself and the label is a tie, broken by convention.

The second form of \(f\) needs only the support vectors and inner products with them. The magnitude \(|f(x_{\text{test}})|/\lVert w\rVert\) is the test point's distance from the boundary, a natural measure of how confident the prediction is.

Part D
Beyond the hard margin
20

Soft margin

The hard-margin SVM has no solution at all if a single point is on the wrong side. Real data needs slack.

Beyond the slides

Blocks 20 and 21 are not in the lecture. They are the two standard extensions that make SVMs usable in practice, and they reuse every idea above.

Give each point a slack variable \(\xi_i\ge0\) that measures how far it falls short of the margin, and charge for it:

$$\min_{w,\,b,\,\xi}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge 1-\xi_i,\quad \xi_i\ge 0$$
  • \(C\) trades width against violations. A large \(C\) makes violations expensive and approaches the hard margin; a small \(C\) accepts some violations in exchange for a wider, more robust band.
  • The dual barely changes. Repeating blocks 14–15 gives the same objective with the box constraint \(0\le\alpha_i\le C\) (plus \(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0\) with a bias).
  • Complementary slackness now has three cases. \(\alpha_i=0\): beyond the margin. \(0<\alpha_i<C\): exactly on the margin. \(\alpha_i=C\): inside the band or misclassified.
  • Hinge loss. At the optimum \(\xi_i=\max\bigl(0,\,1-y_if(x_i)\bigr)\), so the soft-margin SVM is regularised hinge-loss minimisation: \(\min_w\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_i\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))\).
21

Kernels

The dual only ever asks for inner products — so it never needs the features themselves.

In the dual objective and in the prediction rule, the data appears only as \(x_i^{\top}x_j\) and \(x_i^{\top}x_{\text{test}}\). If we first map each point through a feature map \(\phi\), all we need is \(\phi(x_i)^{\top}\phi(x_j)\). A kernel computes that number directly:

$$k(x,z)=\phi(x)^{\top}\phi(z),\qquad f(x_{\text{test}})=\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{SV}}\alpha_i\,y_i\,k(x_i,x_{\text{test}})+b$$
Kernel\(k(x,z)\)Implicit feature space
Linear\(x^{\top}z\)the original features — the SVM of these notes
Polynomial\((x^{\top}z+c)^p\)all monomials up to degree \(p\)
Gaussian (RBF)\(\exp\bigl(-\lVert x-z\rVert^2/2\sigma^2\bigr)\)infinite-dimensional

With the RBF kernel the primal would need an infinite-dimensional \(w\) and cannot even be written down, but the dual is still an \(n\)-variable quadratic program. This is the strongest argument for the dual formulation of block 16. A function is a valid kernel exactly when every Gram matrix it produces is positive semi-definite (Mercer's condition), which keeps the dual concave.

The whole chain in one line

Maximise the margin → fix the scale so the margin is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\) → minimise \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) under affine constraints → strong duality lets us solve the dual instead → stationarity writes \(w\) as a weighted sum of data points → complementary slackness zeroes every weight except those of the support vectors → the dual depends on the data only through inner products, which kernels generalise.
